Q: Late binding in Racket Scheme can't be found in a let-environment A:

Answering your follow-up questions:

define inside a function is called internal definition. The R5RS standard only specifies that implementations must support consecutive internal definitions that appear at the beginning (that is, not interrupted by expressions).

Your first follow-up example, however, doesn't have all internal definitions at the beginning consecutively. (define var 9) is interrupted by the expression (g).

#lang r5rs

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (g)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g))

(f)

Many R5RS implementations simply reject this program as syntactically ill-formed. Try running the above program with e.g. Guile on the site https://ideone.com/.

Racket implementation of R5RS chooses to support this "unrestricted internal definition", but since the standard doesn't say how it should work, there are many possible ways to support it. Racket R5RS goes with one possible behavior: it groups a sequence of consecutive internal definitions together, and break groups into different scopes where a group can refer to definitions in groups preceding it, but not the other way around. I.e., the program is essentially transformed to:

#lang r5rs

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (g)
  (let ()
    (define var 9)
    (display "---") (newline)
    (g)))

(f)

where var in g always refers to the outermost var. This is why it prints 6 .... 6.

In your second follow-up example, (define var 9) is not interrupted, so it follows the standard R5RS semantics, where var in g always refers to var in (define var 9). This is why it prints 9.

#lang r5rs

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  ;(g)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g)
  )

(f)

The actual Racket language (not R5RS) also supports unrestricted internal definition, but with a different behavior from Racket R5RS. var in g always refers to var in (define var 9).

#lang racket

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (g)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g))

(f)

However, the association of the value 9 to var only occurs when the statement is evaluated. Initially, var is uninitialized. Since (g) is called when var is still uninitialized, the evaluation of var results in the runtime error "cannot use before initialization", as you observed.

Using what I described above, we can see that:

#lang r5rs

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (+ 1 1)
  (define var 9)
  (display "---") (newline)
  (g))

(f)

in Racket R5RS would print 6, since (define var 9) is broken up by (+ 1 1), making it effectively transformed to:

#lang r5rs

(define var 6)

(define (f)
  (define g (lambda () (display var) (newline)))
  (+ 1 1)
  (let ()
    (define var 9)
    (display "---") (newline)
    (g)))

(f)

But the same program in #lang racket would print 9, since var in g refers to var in (define var 9), which is already associated with the value 9 by the time g is called.

Q: Why were @, $, and ` not included in C89's basic source character set? A:

It comes down to portability across national variants of ISO 646. These character sets often reassigned ASCII punctuation to local symbols, like swapping # for £.

C89's basic source character set was the bare minimum every compiler had to handle. Since @, $, and ` didn't serve as operators or keywords, I don't think the committee saw any reason to force them into the standard. Leaving them out meant a C program could still compile on systems where those specific code points displayed different glyphs or didn't exist at all.

The C99 UCN carve-out follows that same logic. They were treated as non-portable extras until C23 finally pulled them in. By then, basically every character set in use supported them, so there wasn't much of an obstacle left.

So the committee just waited until the hardware caught up.

Q: Android build failed for kotlin with ksp A:

Thanks @tyg

As per @tyg mention in the post I have update my code also providing another solution for another ksp related issue as below.

As explicit mention kotlin lib in root level build.gradle mismatch kotlin and ksp version after removing below line

//    id 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.android' version '2.3.10' apply false

facing another issue which failed the build

Unresolved reference 'GlideApp' after migrating compiler to ksp for glide in android

If you are also using Glide library update your code in build.gradle as below

//ksp 'com.github.bumptech.glide:compiler:5.0.9' // 
ksp 'com.github.bumptech.glide:ksp:5.0.9'

Turns out that glide ksp compiler should use com.github.bumptech.glide:ksp:$version instead of com.github.bumptech.glide:compiler:$version

Next step if you are using GlideApp then replace GlideApp with Glide, as per migrating with ksp in GlideApp class is deprecated

Old code

GlideApp.with(context)
    .load(url)
    .into(imageView)

New Code

Glide.with(context)
    .load(url)
    .into(imageView)

Q: Will I be able to use Typescript with angular 2.0, or should I use Traceur? A:

Short Answer

Yes, you can and should use TypeScript. Angular (starting from Angular 2.0) is written directly in TypeScript, and TypeScript is the officially recommended language for building Angular applications.

You do not need Traceur. Traceur was used early in Angular 2's development (during the initial experimental stages and the deprecated AtScript experiment), but it was completely replaced by TypeScript.

Detailed Background & Timeline

  1. The Early Phase (AtScript & Traceur):

    • Early in Angular 2.0 design (around 2014), the Angular team explored AtScript, an extension of ES6 using Google’s Traceur compiler to transpile ES6 annotations and types down to ES5.

  2. The Collaboration with Microsoft (ng-conf 2015):

    • At ng-conf 2015, the Angular team and Microsoft announced that AtScript and TypeScript would converge.

    • Microsoft added support for decorators/metadata annotations (ES7 proposal) and improved type checking in TypeScript (starting in TypeScript 1.5+).

    • As a result, Google dropped AtScript and Traceur, rewriting Angular 2 entirely in TypeScript.

Why TypeScript is the Standard for Angular

  • First-Class Support & Tooling: TypeScript provides native support for decorators (@Component, @Injectable, etc.), static typing, compile-time error checking, and IDE autocompletion (IntelliSense).

  • Direct Alignment with Modern ECMAScript: TypeScript is a strict superset of ECMAScript. It continuously adopts modern JavaScript features while offering type safety.

  • Traceur is Obsolete: Traceur was an early experimental ES6-to-ES5 transpiler. Today, modern builds use TypeScript (tsc), Babel, or bundler-integrated transpilers (e.g., SWC/esbuild/Vite/Webpack), making Traceur unnecessary.
